claim: Fabp7 (BLBP) is approximately 140-fold enriched in satellite glial cells compared to other ganglionic cell types in adult mouse sympathetic and sensory ganglia.
source: Using data sets from our recently published single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of peripheral sympathetic and sensory ganglia from adult mice (postnatal days 30–45) (Mapps et al., 2022), we found that BLBP (Fabp7) is ~140-fold enriched in satellite glial cells compared to other ganglionic cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data from the authors' published work (Mapps et al., 2022) and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BLBP-positive satellite glia form thin ring-like glial sheaths around neuronal somas by 2 weeks after birth in mouse sympathetic ganglia.
source: However, by 2 weeks after birth, BLBP-positive satellite glial cells had expanded processes around neuronal cell bodies and formed thin ring-like glial sheaths around neuronal somas when observed at P31 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing BLBP and TH labeling at different developmental time points, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment in Fabp7-CreER2;ROSA26mEGFP mice results in m-EGFP reporter expression in satellite glia marked by Kir4.1 immunolabeling, but not in TH-positive sympathetic neurons, IBA1-labeled macrophages, or Pdgfrβ-labeled vascular mural cells.
source: We found that tamoxifen treatment (180 mg/kg body weight for five consecutive days) in Fabp7-CreER2;ROSA26mEGFP mice resulted in m-EGFP reporter expression in satellite glia marked by Kir4.1 immunolabeling (Vit et al., 2006), but not in TH-positive sympathetic neurons, IBA1-labeled macrophages, or Pdgfrβ-labeled vascular mural cells in sympathetic ganglia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data from Fabp7-CreER2;ROSA26mEGFP reporter mice showing co-localization with Kir4.1 but not with other cell type markers, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–F. The Kir4.1 marker is supported by citation to Vit et al., 2006.

claim: There is a threefold increase in TUNEL-positive cells in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic ganglia compared to controls at 5 days post-tamoxifen injection.
source: To determine whether DTA expression results in cell death, we assessed apoptosis using TUNEL labeling and observed a threefold increase in TUNEL-positive cells in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic ganglia compared to controls at 5 days post-tamoxifen injection (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL labeling data quantified in Figure 1C and D showing increased apoptosis at 5 dpi.

claim: There is a twofold increase in the number of TUNEL+;Sox10+ cells in BLBP:iDTA ganglia compared to controls at 5 days post-tamoxifen injection.
source: We found a twofold increase in the number of TUNEL+;Sox10+ cells in BLBP:iDTA ganglia compared to controls at 5 days post-tamoxifen injection (5 dpi) (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-labeling of TUNEL and Sox10 immunostaining data quantified in Figure 1E–G.

claim: The number of TUNEL+;TrkA+ sympathetic neurons in BLBP:iDTA ganglia was not statistically different from that in controls at 5 days post-tamoxifen injection.
source: Although there was a trend toward enhanced neuronal apoptosis, the number of TUNEL+;TrkA+ sympathetic neurons in BLBP:iDTA ganglia was not statistically different from that in controls at this stage (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and TrkA co-labeling data quantified in Figure 1F–H showing no significant difference at 5 dpi.

claim: There is a 54.2% decrease in Sox2-labeled satellite glial cells in sympathetic ganglia from BLBP:iDTA mice at 14 days post-tamoxifen injection.
source: By 14 days post-tamoxifen injection (14 dpi), however, there was a pronounced loss of Sox2-labeled satellite glial cells (54.2% decrease) in sympathetic ganglia from BLBP:iDTA mice (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sox2 immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 1I and J at 14 dpi.

claim: There is a significant loss of glial nuclei associated with soma of individual sympathetic neurons in BLBP:iDTA mice compared to control mice at 14 dpi.
source: We observed a significant loss of glial nuclei associated with soma of individual sympathetic neurons in BLBP:iDTA mice compared to control mice at 14 dpi (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by TH DAB immunohistochemistry and hematoxylin staining data quantified in Figure 1K and L.

claim: Satellite glia are undergoing apoptosis by 5 dpi, and by 14 dpi, there is a substantial loss of glial cells in BLBP:iDTA ganglia.
source: Together, these results indicate that satellite glia are undergoing apoptosis by 5 dpi, and by 14 dpi, there is a substantial loss of glial cells in BLBP:iDTA ganglia.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on multiple pieces of data presented in the manuscript, including TUNEL labeling at 5 dpi and Sox2 quantification at 14 dpi.

claim: There is a pronounced downregulation of several satellite glia-specific transcripts, including Fabp7, Fasn, Apoe, and Kcnj10, in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic ganglia at 14 dpi.
source: Further, consistent with cell loss at 14 dpi, we found a pronounced downregulation of several satellite glia-specific transcripts, including Fabp7, Fasn, Apoe, and Kcnj10 (Mapps et al., 2022), in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic ganglia at this time as revealed by quantitative PCR (qPCR) analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H. The identification of these transcripts as satellite glia-specific is supported by citation to Mapps et al., 2022.

claim: In BLBP:iDTA ganglia, there was no increased macrophage infiltration as assessed by quantification of IBA-1-labeled cells.
source: In BLBP:iDTA ganglia, we did not find increased macrophage infiltration as assessed by quantification of IBA-1-labeled cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IBA-1 immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: EdU labeling indicated that satellite glial cells do not undergo increased proliferation as a compensatory or injury-induced response after DTA expression.
source: Further, EdU labeling indicated that satellite glial cells do not undergo increased proliferation as a compensatory or injury-induced response after DTA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: DTA-induced ablation of satellite glia is not accompanied by increased macrophage density or glial proliferation in mutant sympathetic ganglia.
source: Together, these results suggest that DTA-induced ablation of satellite glia is not accompanied by increased macrophage density or glial proliferation in mutant sympathetic ganglia.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the IBA-1 and EdU labeling data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is a drastic downregulation in Th and Dopamine Beta-Hydroxylase (DBH) transcript levels (88 and 99% decrease, respectively) in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic ganglia.
source: qPCR analyses revealed a drastic downregulation in Th and Dopamine Beta-Hydroxylase (DBH) transcript levels, (88 and 99% decrease, respectively) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: DBH converts dopamine to NE in the NE biosynthetic pathway.
source: DBH converts dopamine to NE in the NE biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical knowledge about the norepinephrine biosynthetic pathway.

claim: Satellite glia maintain noradrenergic enzymes in sympathetic neurons.
source: Thus, satellite glia maintain noradrenergic enzymes in sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that noradrenergic enzyme expression is downregulated when satellite glia are ablated.

claim: Median values for soma areas are 162 ± 17 μm2 for control neurons vs 118 ± 7.1 μm2 for mutant neurons at 5 dpi.
source: Median values for soma areas are 162 ± 17 μm2 for control neurons vs 118 ± 7.1 μm2 for mutant neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of soma sizes from TH immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a dramatic reduction in p-S6 and p-4-EBP1 immunoreactivity in satellite glia-depleted ganglia.
source: We observed a dramatic reduction in p-S6 and p-4-EBP1 immunoreactivity in satellite glia-depleted ganglia (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data for p-S6 and p-4-EBP1 shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Satellite glia promote soma growth, in part, via regulating mTOR signaling in sympathetic neurons.
source: These results suggest that satellite glia promote soma growth, in part, via regulating mTOR signaling in sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mTOR pathway effectors (p-S6 and p-4-EBP1) are reduced in satellite glia-depleted ganglia, which also show soma atrophy.

claim: At 5 dpi, sympathetic neuron numbers in BLBP:iDTA mice were not significantly different from that in control littermates (12,240 ± 1514 in mutant vs. 14,200 ± 1005 in control mice).
source: At 5 dpi, sympathetic neuron numbers in BLBP:iDTA mice were not significantly different from that in control littermates (12,240 ± 1514 in mutant vs. 14,200 ± 1005 in control mice) as revealed by Nissl staining and quantification of cell counts in tissue sections from SCG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nissl staining and cell count data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: By 14 dpi, there is a marked loss of sympathetic neurons (24% decrease) in satellite glia-ablated ganglia (11,790 ± 706 mutant neurons vs. 15,460 ± 734 control neurons).
source: However, by 14 dpi, we found a marked loss of sympathetic neurons (24% decrease) in satellite glia-ablated ganglia (11,790 ± 706 mutant neurons vs. 15,460 ± 734 control neurons) (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nissl staining and cell count data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Sympathetic axon innervation was maintained in target organs in BLBP:iDTA mice, when assessed by wholemount TH immunostaining in iDISCO-cleared tissues and light sheet microscopy.
source: Despite the decrease in neuronal numbers, sympathetic axon innervation was maintained in target organs in BLBP:iDTA mice, when assessed by wholemount TH immunostaining in iDISCO-cleared tissues and light sheet microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by iDISCO-based tissue clearing and wholemount TH immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: TH levels in mutant axons appeared to be similar to that in controls, despite the marked reduction in Th mRNA and protein in neuronal cell bodies residing in the ganglia.
source: Intriguingly, TH levels in mutant axons appeared to be similar to that in controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E), despite the marked reduction in Th mRNA and protein in neuronal cell bodies residing in the ganglia (see Figure 2A and B), suggesting differential regulation of TH distribution in neuronal soma vs. axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of TH immunostaining in axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E) versus soma (Figure 2A and B).

claim: Satellite glia provide trophic and metabolic support to adult sympathetic neurons and regulate noradrenergic biosynthetic machinery, specifically in neuronal cell bodies.
source: Together, these results indicate that satellite glia provide trophic and metabolic support to adult sympathetic neurons and regulate noradrenergic biosynthetic machinery, specifically in neuronal cell bodies.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations including soma atrophy, impaired mTOR signaling, neuronal loss, and downregulated noradrenergic enzymes in satellite glia-depleted mice.

claim: BLBP:iDTA mice have increased basal pupil areas compared to controls.
source: Surprisingly, despite the neuronal loss and downregulated noradrenergic biosynthetic enzymes in neuronal soma, we observed increased basal pupil areas in BLBP:iDTA mice compared to controls (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pupil size measurements shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Light onset at 0.1 lux or higher resulted in rapid constriction with greater constrictions at higher light intensities in both BLBP:iDTA and control mice.
source: Light onset at 0.1 lux or higher resulted in rapid constriction with greater constrictions at higher light intensities in both BLBP:iDTA and control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pupil constriction measurements in response to light shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The intensity responses for pupil constriction were virtually identical for BLBP:iDTA and control groups.
source: The intensity responses were virtually identical for the two groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of pupil constriction responses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Parasympathetic function is intact in BLBP:iDTA mice.
source: These results suggest that parasympathetic function is intact in BLBP:iDTA mice and that the enlarged pupil areas likely reflect an increase in sympathetic tone with the loss of satellite glia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that pupil constriction in response to light is normal in BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: BLBP:iDTA mice exhibit elevated heart rate compared to controls.
source: Strikingly, BLBP:iDTA mice exhibited increased heart rates (Figure 3C and D) and decreased HRV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECG recordings shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: BLBP:iDTA mice exhibit decreased heart rate variability (HRV) compared to controls.
source: Strikingly, BLBP:iDTA mice exhibited increased heart rates (Figure 3C and D) and decreased HRV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECG recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tamoxifen injections had no effect on heart rate in wild-type C57BL/6J mice or control ROSA26eGFP-DTA mice that do not express Cre.
source: Tamoxifen injections had no effect on heart rate in wild-type C57BL/6J mice or control ROSA26eGFP-DTA mice that do not express Cre (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECG recordings from tamoxifen-treated control mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Ablation of sympathetic nerves using 6-OHDA prevented the augmented heart rate in BLBP:iDTA mice.
source: Ablation of sympathetic nerves prevented the augmented heart rate in BLBP:iDTA mice (Figure 3E and F), suggesting the dysfunction of peripheral sympathetic neurons as the primary contributor to the cardiac defect in satellite glia-ablated mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by ECG recordings after 6-OHDA treatment shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: 6-OHDA selectively destroys sympathetic, but not parasympathetic or sensory nerves.
source: To directly test the involvement of sympathetic neurons in the heart defect observed in BLBP:iDTA mice, we chemically ablated sympathetic nerves using 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA), which selectively destroys sympathetic, but not parasympathetic or sensory nerves (Borden et al., 2013; Kostrzewa and Jacobowitz, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Borden et al., 2013 and Kostrzewa and Jacobowitz, 1974.

claim: 6-OHDA does not cross the blood–brain barrier after intraperitoneal injections in adult animals, restricting its actions to the periphery.
source: Further, 6-OHDA does not cross the blood–brain barrier after intraperitoneal injections in adult animals, restricting its actions to the periphery (Kostrzewa and Jacobowitz, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kostrzewa and Jacobowitz, 1974.

claim: There is a significant 1.6-fold increase in circulating NE levels in BLBP:iDTA mice compared to controls.
source: To understand the molecular and/or cellular basis for enhanced sympathetic activity in satellite glia-depleted mice, we measured circulating NE levels and observed a significant 1.6-fold increase in BLBP:iDTA mice compared to controls (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by NE ELISA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There is significantly decreased expression of Adrb1, Adrb2, and Adra2c in cardiac tissue from BLBP:iDTA mice.
source: We found significantly decreased expression of Adrb1, the major adrenergic receptor for NE signaling in the heart (de Lucia et al., 2018), as well as Adrb2 and Adra2c, using qPCR analyses of cardiac tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from cardiac tissue shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E. The identification of Adrb1 as the major adrenergic receptor in the heart is supported by citation to de Lucia et al., 2018.

claim: There is a striking eightfold increase in the number of c-Fos-positive sympathetic neurons in BLBP:iDTA ganglia compared to controls.
source: Lastly, immunostaining for c-Fos, an immediate early transcription factor that serves as a reporter of neuronal activity (Sheng and Greenberg, 1990), revealed a striking eightfold increase in the number of c-Fos-positive sympathetic neurons in BLBP:iDTA ganglia compared to controls (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H and I. The characterization of c-Fos as a reporter of neuronal activity is supported by citation to Sheng and Greenberg, 1990.

claim: Satellite glia depletion results in elevated sympathetic neuron activity, impaired NE homeostasis, and autonomic behavioral defects in mice.
source: Together, these results indicate that satellite glia depletion results in elevated sympathetic neuron activity, impaired NE homeostasis, and autonomic behavioral defects in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations including increased c-Fos expression, elevated circulating NE, increased pupil size, and elevated heart rate in BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: Kcnj10 mRNA for Kir4.1 is highly enriched in satellite glia (approximately threefold enriched) compared to other ganglionic cell types based on single-cell RNA-sequencing of sympathetic and sensory ganglia from adult mice.
source: Kcnj10 mRNA for Kir4.1 is highly enriched in satellite glia (approximately threefold enriched) compared to other ganglionic cell types based on our analysis of data sets obtained from single-cell RNA-sequencing of sympathetic and sensory ganglia from adult mice (postnatal days 30–45) (Mapps et al., 2022; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data from Mapps et al., 2022 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In BLBP:iDTA sympathetic ganglia, there is a pronounced decrease in Kcnj10 mRNA compared to controls as assessed by qPCR analysis and single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH).
source: Further, in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic ganglia, we observed a pronounced decrease in Kcnj10 mRNA compared to controls as assessed by qPCR analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H) and single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H) and smFISH data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Global or tissue-specific Kir4.1 deletion in mice results in impaired K+ and glutamate homeostasis, loss of glial K+ conductance, neuronal excitability, epileptic seizures, and pain-like behaviors.
source: In mice, global or tissue-specific Kir4.1 deletion results in impaired K+ and glutamate homeostasis, loss of glial K+ conductance, neuronal excitability, epileptic seizures, and pain-like behaviors (Cui et al., 2018; Djukic et al., 2007; Olsen et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2010; Vit et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2018; Djukic et al., 2007; Olsen et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2010; Vit et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of Kir4.1 was significantly reduced in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia, with qPCR analysis indicating a 76% decrease in Kcnj10 transcript levels.
source: Expression of Kir4.1, visualized by immunofluorescence, was significantly reduced in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia (Figure 4A), and qPCR analysis indicated a 76% decrease in Kcnj10 transcript levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kir4.1 immunostaining (Figure 4A) and qPCR data (Figure 4B).

claim: Loss of Kir4.1 did not alter satellite glial numbers in sympathetic ganglia as assessed by quantification of Sox2-positive cells.
source: Loss of Kir4.1 did not alter satellite glial numbers in sympathetic ganglia as assessed by quantification of Sox2-positive cells (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sox2 immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4C and D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Kir4.1 deletion did not affect Fabp7 (BLBP) expression in satellite glia assessed by qPCR analysis and immunostaining.
source: Kir4.1 deletion also did not affect Fabp7 (BLBP) expression in satellite glia assessed by qPCR analysis and immunostaining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and BLBP immunostaining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The characteristic ring-like glial organization around neuronal soma was not perturbed in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia.
source: BLBP immunostaining also indicated that the characteristic ring-like glial organization around neuronal soma was not perturbed in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLBP immunostaining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: There is a marked increase in the number of c-Fos-positive cells in Kir4.1 cKO SCGs compared to controls.
source: However, we observed a marked increase in the number of c-Fos-positive cells in Kir4.1 cKO SCGs compared to controls (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The majority of c-Fos-positive cells in Kir4.1 cKO ganglia appeared to be neurons based on their morphology.
source: The majority of c-Fos-positive cells in Kir4.1 cKO ganglia appeared to be neurons based on their morphology.
evidence: This is an observation based on morphological assessment of c-Fos-positive cells.

claim: Kir4.1 deletion resulted in downregulated expression of noradrenergic biosynthetic enzymes, TH and DBH, in neuronal cell bodies.
source: Intriguingly, despite increased c-Fos-positive sympathetic neurons, Kir4.1 deletion resulted in downregulated expression of noradrenergic biosynthetic enzymes, TH and DBH, in neuronal cell bodies (Figure 4C, G, and H), similar to the phenotype observed with satellite glia depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by TH immunostaining (Figure 4C) and qPCR data for TH and DBH (Figure 4G and H).

claim: Satellite glial cells control sympathetic neuron activity and noradrenergic enzyme expression via Kir4.1-dependent regulation of the neuronal microenvironment.
source: Together, these results suggest that satellite glial cells control sympathetic neuron activity and noradrenergic enzyme expression via Kir4.1-dependent regulation of the neuronal microenvironment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kir4.1 deletion in satellite glia results in increased neuronal activity and downregulated noradrenergic enzymes.

claim: Kir4.1 loss in satellite glial cells elicited a pronounced decrease in the levels of p-S6 and p-4-EBP1 in sympathetic neurons.
source: Kir4.1 loss in satellite glial cells also elicited a pronounced decrease in the levels of p-S6 and p-4-EBP1, two well-established downstream effectors of mTOR activity (Meyuhas, 2008; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017), in sympathetic neurons (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), similar to the effects of satellite glia ablation (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by p-S6 and p-4-EBP1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A. The characterization of p-S6 and p-4-EBP1 as mTOR effectors is supported by citations to Meyuhas, 2008 and Saxton and Sabatini, 2017.

claim: There is an eightfold increase in apoptotic cells in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia using TUNEL labeling at 14 days post-tamoxifen injection.
source: Notably, we observed an eightfold increase in apoptotic cells in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia using TUNEL labeling at 14 days post-tamoxifen injection (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL labeling data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The apoptotic cells in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia were primarily sympathetic neurons based on co-labeling for TUNEL and TrkA.
source: The apoptotic cells were primarily sympathetic neurons based on co-labeling for TUNEL and TrkA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and TrkA co-labeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: There was no increased apoptosis of satellite glial cells in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia compared to controls.
source: We did not observe increased apoptosis of satellite glial cells in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E), consistent with results that the number of Sox2-positive satellite glia was not altered by Kir4.1 deletion (see Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and Sox10 co-labeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: There is a 22% decrease in sympathetic neuron numbers in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia by 2 weeks after tamoxifen injections.
source: Consistent with enhanced neuronal apoptosis, we observed a 22% decrease in sympathetic neuron numbers in Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic ganglia by 2 weeks after tamoxifen injections (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nissl staining and cell count data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Sympathetic axon innervation and axonal TH expression were similar between Kir4.1 cKO mice and controls.
source: Similar to the findings in BLBP:iDTA mice, sympathetic axon innervation and axonal TH expression were similar between Kir4.1 cKO mice and controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G), despite the decrease in sympathetic neuron numbers and downregulated TH expression in neuronal cell bodies.
evidence: The claim is supported by TH immunostaining and quantification of innervation in salivary glands shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Kir4.1 is necessary for the survival of adult sympathetic neurons.
source: Together, these results highlight that Kir4.1 is necessary for the survival of adult sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kir4.1 deletion in satellite glia results in increased neuronal apoptosis and decreased neuron numbers.

claim: Basal pupil size, heart rate, and circulating NE levels were not significantly altered in Kir4.1 cKO mice.
source: Measurements of basal pupil size, heart rate, and circulating NE levels indicated that these parameters were not significantly altered in Kir4.1 cKO mice (Figure 5H and I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–J), despite increased neuronal activity as assessed by c-Fos immunoreactivity (see Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by pupil size measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–I), ECG recordings (Figure 5H and I), and NE ELISA data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).

claim: Parasympathetic activity assessed by pupil constriction in response to different light intensities was normal in Kir4.1 cKO mice.
source: Parasympathetic activity assessed by pupil constriction in response to different light intensities was also normal in Kir4.1 cKO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by pupil constriction measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Kir4.1 deletion recapitulates the cellular phenotypes observed in BLBP:iDTA mice, notably, increased neuron activity, impaired metabolic signaling, and enhanced apoptosis.
source: Together, these results suggest that Kir4.1 deletion recapitulates the cellular phenotypes observed in BLBP:iDTA mice, notably, increased neuron activity, impaired metabolic signaling, and enhanced apoptosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of phenotypes between Kir4.1 cKO and BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: The deletion of a single gene, Kcnj10 encoding for Kir4.1, from satellite glial cells is not sufficient to drive behavioral changes at the whole animal level as seen with genetic ablation of satellite glial cells.
source: However, the deletion of a single gene, Kcnj10 encoding for Kir4.1, from satellite glial cells is not sufficient to drive behavioral changes at the whole animal level as seen with genetic ablation of satellite glial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kir4.1 cKO mice do not show the autonomic behavioral defects (increased pupil size, heart rate, circulating NE) seen in BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: There are other satellite glia-dependent mechanisms, in addition to Kir4.1 activity, that contribute to regulation of neuronal excitability to drive circuit-level changes.
source: These results suggest that there are other satellite glia-dependent mechanisms, in addition to Kir4.1 activity, that contribute to regulation of neuronal excitability to drive circuit-level changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kir4.1 deletion alone does not fully recapitulate the behavioral phenotypes of satellite glia ablation.

claim: Satellite glia modulate sympathetic neuron metabolism, survival, neurotransmitter homeostasis, activity, and autonomic functions in adult mice.
source: Here, we show that satellite glia modulate sympathetic neuron metabolism, survival, neurotransmitter homeostasis, activity, and autonomic functions in adult mice.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons and their surrounding glial covers are functional units in the regulation of sympathetic output.
source: Together, our findings provide in vivo evidence that neurons and their surrounding glial covers are functional units in the regulation of sympathetic output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective findings that satellite glia regulate multiple aspects of sympathetic neuron function and autonomic behaviors.

claim: A key role for satellite glia is in restraining neuronal activity in mature sympathetic neurons.
source: We reveal that a key role for satellite glia is in restraining neuronal activity in mature sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that satellite glia depletion results in increased neuronal activity (c-Fos expression) and elevated sympathetic tone.

claim: Depletion of satellite glia in adult mice amplifies neuronal activity, leading to increased circulating levels of NE and elevated sympathetic tone.
source: Depletion of satellite glia in adult mice amplifies neuronal activity, leading to increased circulating levels of NE and elevated sympathetic tone.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased c-Fos expression, elevated circulating NE, increased pupil size, and elevated heart rate in BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: Glia-ablated mice show enhanced pupil size and heart rate, demonstrating the necessity of these cells in the dynamic regulation of autonomic functions in conscious and freely moving animals.
source: Glia-ablated mice show enhanced pupil size and heart rate, demonstrating the necessity of these cells in the dynamic regulation of autonomic functions in conscious and freely moving animals.
evidence: This is supported by pupil size and ECG data from BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: Satellite glia limit neuronal activity, similar to reported functions of other glial cells that encapsulate neuronal cell bodies, in particular, astrocytes, microglia, and cortex glia in Drosophila.
source: Our findings that satellite glia limit neuronal activity are similar to reported functions of other glial cells that encapsulate neuronal cell bodies, in particular, astrocytes (Allen and Lyons, 2018), microglia (Badimon et al., 2020; Cserép et al., 2020), and cortex glia in Drosophila (Yadav et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to published literature supported by citations to Allen and Lyons, 2018; Badimon et al., 2020; Cserép et al., 2020; and Yadav et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibitory effects of satellite glia might enable sympathetic neurons to respond to a wider range of input strengths and/or serve as a neuroprotective mechanism to limit neurotoxicity under conditions of stress or pathology.
source: Inhibitory effects of satellite glia might enable sympathetic neurons to respond to a wider range of input strengths and/or serve as a neuroprotective mechanism to limit neurotoxicity under conditions of stress or pathology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functional implications of satellite glia's inhibitory effects.

claim: Glial regulation of ion homeostasis, specifically K+ clearance, is a key mechanism that contributes to inhibition of neuronal activity.
source: The enhanced neuronal c-Fos signals in Kir4.1 cKO and satellite glia-ablated mice suggest that glial regulation of ion homeostasis, specifically, K+ clearance, is a key mechanism that contributes to inhibition of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both satellite glia ablation and Kir4.1 deletion result in increased neuronal activity.

claim: Satellite glia have high K+ conductance, which is almost exclusively dependent on Kir4.1 expression.
source: Electrophysiological analyses show that satellite glia have high K+ conductance, which is almost exclusively dependent on Kir4.1 expression (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2010.

claim: Satellite glial cells are coupled to one another through gap junctions.
source: Satellite glial cells are also coupled to one another through gap junctions (Huang et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2005 and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Kir4.1 or Connexin 43 enhances excitability of sensory neurons and evokes nociceptive responses in rats.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Kir4.1 or Connexin 43, a gap junction protein, enhances excitability of sensory neurons and evokes nociceptive responses in rats (Ohara et al., 2008; Vit et al., 2008; Ohara et al., 2008; Vit et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ohara et al., 2008 and Vit et al., 2008.

claim: Satellite glia are capable of taking up extracellular K+, distributing them throughout a glial syncytium via gap junction coupling, and extruding ions in regions of low K+ concentration, in a process called 'spatial K+ buffering'.
source: Together, these studies suggest that satellite glia are capable of taking up extracellular K+, distributing them throughout a glial syncytium via gap junction coupling, and extruding ions in regions of low K+ concentration, in a process called 'spatial K+ buffering' (Kuffler, 1967; Tang et al., 2010), similar to astrocyte functions in the CNS (Kofuji and Newman, 2004).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on published literature, supported by citations to Kuffler, 1967; Tang et al., 2010; and Kofuji and Newman, 2004.

claim: Even slight elevations in extracellular K+ in the neuronal microenvironment, due to loss of glial Kir4.1, are likely to elicit neuronal depolarization and activation.
source: Even slight elevations in extracellular K+ in the neuronal microenvironment, due to loss of glial Kir4.1, are likely to elicit neuronal depolarization and activation (Cui et al., 2018; Haydon, 2001).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citations to Cui et al., 2018 and Haydon, 2001.

claim: Kir4.1 is a major contributor to the hyperpolarized resting membrane potential of satellite glia.
source: For example, Kir4.1 is a major contributor to the hyperpolarized resting membrane potential of satellite glia (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2010.

claim: Depolarization of satellite glia, induced by loss of Kir4.1, could likely affect voltage-dependent processes in these cells.
source: Depolarization of satellite glia, induced by loss of Kir4.1, could likely affect voltage-dependent processes in these cells (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms, supported by citation to Tang et al., 2010.

claim: Kir4.1, expressed in astrocytes, inhibits the synthesis of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in astrocytes.
source: Kir4.1, expressed in astrocytes, inhibits the synthesis of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in astrocytes (Kinboshi et al., 2017; Ohno et al., 2018), and astrocyte-derived BDNF has been shown to enhance neuronal activity through presynaptic mechanisms in the ventromedial hypothalamus (Ameroso et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kinboshi et al., 2017; Ohno et al., 2018; and Ameroso et al., 2022.

claim: An analogous Kir4.1-BDNF pathway might operate in satellite glia to influence neuron activity since BDNF is known to increase presynaptic input to post-ganglionic sympathetic neurons in sympathetic ganglia.
source: Thus, an analogous Kir4.1-BDNF pathway might operate in satellite glia to influence neuron activity since BDNF is known to increase presynaptic input to post-ganglionic sympathetic neurons in sympathetic ganglia (Causing et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms in satellite glia, with the BDNF effect in sympathetic ganglia supported by citation to Causing et al., 1997.

claim: Satellite glia-specific loss of Kir4.1 recapitulates all the cellular phenotypes observed in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic neurons, specifically, increased neuronal activity, diminished mTOR signaling, soma atrophy, downregulated expression of noradrenergic enzymes, and neuronal apoptosis.
source: We found that satellite glia-specific loss of Kir4.1 recapitulates all the cellular phenotypes observed in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic neurons, specifically, increased neuronal activity, diminished mTOR signaling, soma atrophy, downregulated expression of noradrenergic enzymes, and neuronal apoptosis.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on comparison of phenotypes between Kir4.1 cKO and BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: Additional glia-dependent mechanisms must contribute to neuronal excitability to drive network-level changes beyond Kir4.1.
source: Thus, additional glia-dependent mechanisms must contribute to neuronal excitability to drive network-level changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kir4.1 deletion does not fully recapitulate the behavioral phenotypes of satellite glia ablation.

claim: Satellite glia could influence neuronal activity via regulation of ganglionic levels of acetylcholine, the major neurotransmitter released by pre-ganglionic axons.
source: Satellite glia could influence neuronal activity via regulation of ganglionic levels of acetylcholine, the major neurotransmitter released by pre-ganglionic axons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Satellite glia modulate cholinergic neurotransmission in co-cultured sympathetic neurons.
source: Despite previous observations that satellite glia modulate cholinergic neurotransmission in co-cultured sympathetic neurons (Enes et al., 2020; Feldman-Goriachnik et al., 2018), we did not detect glial transcripts involved in cholinergic signaling using single-cell RNA-sequencing of sympathetic ganglia (Mapps et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim about modulation in co-culture is supported by citations to Enes et al., 2020 and Feldman-Goriachnik et al., 2018. The lack of detection in single-cell RNA-seq is supported by citation to Mapps et al., 2022.

claim: Another potential mechanism could involve glial regulation of extracellular ATP and/or its breakdown products in the neuronal microenvironment.
source: Another potential mechanism could involve glial regulation of extracellular ATP and/or its breakdown products in the neuronal microenvironment (Hanani, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms, with general context supported by citation to Hanani, 2010.

claim: In sympathetic ganglia, ATP is largely released by innervating cholinergic pre-ganglionic axons and facilitates fast excitatory neurotransmission in post-ganglionic sympathetic neurons.
source: In sympathetic ganglia, ATP is largely released by innervating cholinergic pre-ganglionic axons and facilitates fast excitatory neurotransmission in post-ganglionic sympathetic neurons (Boehm, 1999; Evans et al., 1992; McCaman and McAfee, 1986; Vizi et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boehm, 1999; Evans et al., 1992; McCaman and McAfee, 1986; and Vizi et al., 1997.

claim: Extracellular ATP is rapidly metabolized by cell-surface ectonucleotidases, which are expressed in sympathetic satellite glia.
source: Extracellular ATP is rapidly metabolized by cell-surface ectonucleotidases, which are expressed in sympathetic satellite glia (Forsman and Elfvin, 1984; Nacimiento et al., 1991; Vizi et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forsman and Elfvin, 1984; Nacimiento et al., 1991; and Vizi et al., 1997.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing data revealed several transcripts involved in ATP sensing, hydrolysis, and removal of breakdown products in sympathetic satellite glia, including P2rx4, P2rx7, P2ry12, Entpd1, and Adk.
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing data revealed several transcripts involved in ATP sensing, hydrolysis, and removal of breakdown products in sympathetic satellite glia, including the purinergic receptors, P2rx4, P2rx7, and P2ry12, and Entpd1, an ectoenzyme which catalyzes ATP to ADP hydrolysis, as well as Adk (adenosine kinase) (Mapps et al., 2022), which is best known for mediating astrocytic uptake of extracellular adenosine in the brain (Boison et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data from Mapps et al., 2022. The function of Adk in astrocytes is supported by citation to Boison et al., 2010.

claim: Autonomic defects observed in BLBP:iDTA mice arise primarily from defects in peripheral sympathetic neurons.
source: Our results suggest that autonomic defects observed in BLBP:iDTA mice arise primarily from defects in peripheral sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 6-OHDA rescue experiment and other control experiments.

claim: 6-OHDA-mediated ablation of sympathetic nerves prevents elevated heart rate in BLBP:iDTA mice.
source: We demonstrate that 6-OHDA-mediated ablation of sympathetic nerves prevents elevated heart rate in BLBP:iDTA mice.
evidence: This is supported by ECG data after 6-OHDA treatment shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Since 6-OHDA selectively destroys sympathetic nerves, these results exclude the involvement of sensory or parasympathetic neurons to the cardiac defect in BLBP:iDTA mice.
source: Since 6-OHDA selectively destroys sympathetic nerves (Kostrzewa and Jacobowitz, 1974), these results exclude the involvement of sensory or parasympathetic neurons to the cardiac defect in BLBP:iDTA mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 6-OHDA rescue experiment and the known selectivity of 6-OHDA (supported by citation to Kostrzewa and Jacobowitz, 1974).

claim: Parasympathetic function in BLBP:iDTA mice appears to be unaffected since mutant mice fully constrict their pupils in response to light.
source: Parasympathetic function in BLBP:iDTA mice appears to be unaffected since mutant mice fully constrict their pupils in response to light.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pupil constriction data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BLBP is expressed in neuronal progenitors, radial glia, and astrocytes in the CNS.
source: BLBP is also expressed in neuronal progenitors, radial glia, and astrocytes in the CNS (Ebrahimi et al., 2016; Feng et al., 1994; Matsumata et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ebrahimi et al., 2016; Feng et al., 1994; and Matsumata et al., 2012.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis indicates an approximately 45-fold enrichment of Fabp7 transcript in satellite glia relative to astrocytes.
source: Our single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of satellite glia (Mapps et al., 2022) compared to published single-cell RNA studies of astrocytes (Batiuk et al., 2020) indicates an ~45-fold enrichment of Fabp7 transcript in satellite glia relative to astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of single-cell RNA-seq data from Mapps et al., 2022 and Batiuk et al., 2020.

claim: Astrocyte ablation in adult mice results in severe motor deficits, including limb paralysis, ataxia, as well as smaller body weight.
source: Further, astrocyte ablation in adult mice results in severe motor deficits, including limb paralysis, ataxia, as well as smaller body weight (Schreiner et al., 2015), none of which were observed in BLBP:iDTA mice.
evidence: The claim about astrocyte ablation phenotypes is supported by citation to Schreiner et al., 2015. The lack of these phenotypes in BLBP:iDTA mice is an observation from the current study.

claim: Astrocyte-specific deletion of Kcnj10 using GFAP-cre mice results in premature lethality, epileptic seizures, and severe ataxia.
source: Similarly, astrocyte-specific deletion of Kcnj10 using GFAP-cre mice results in premature lethality, epileptic seizures, and severe ataxia (Djukic et al., 2007), none of which were observed with Kir4.1 deletion using Fabp7-CreER2 mice.
evidence: The claim about astrocyte-specific Kcnj10 deletion phenotypes is supported by citation to Djukic et al., 2007. The lack of these phenotypes in Kir4.1 cKO mice is an observation from the current study.

claim: Astrocytes are minimally perturbed in BLBP:iDTA and Kir4.1 cKO mice.
source: Together, these results suggest that astrocytes are minimally perturbed in BLBP:iDTA and Kir4.1 cKO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of CNS phenotypes typically associated with astrocyte dysfunction.

claim: Chemogenetic manipulation of satellite glia by activating a Gq-GPCR signaling pathway increased heart rate in Gfap-hM3Dq mice.
source: In a previous study, chemogenetic manipulation of satellite glia by activating a Gq-GPCR signaling pathway increased heart rate in Gfap-hM3Dq mice (Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2017.

claim: Sympathetic satellite glia, very likely, exert both excitatory and inhibitory effects on neuronal activity in a context-dependent manner, similar to astrocyte functions in the brain.
source: Nevertheless, sympathetic satellite glia, very likely, exert both excitatory and inhibitory effects on neuronal activity in a context-dependent manner, similar to astrocyte functions in the brain (Allen and Lyons, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential dual functions of satellite glia, with comparison to astrocytes supported by citation to Allen and Lyons, 2018.

claim: Under conditions of nerve injury or inflammation, activated sensory satellite glia are known to undergo structural and functional changes, resulting in neuronal hyper-excitability.
source: Specifically, under conditions of nerve injury or inflammation, activated sensory satellite glia are known to undergo structural and functional changes, resulting in neuronal hyper-excitability (Hanani and Spray, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hanani and Spray, 2020.

claim: In response to nerve damage, sympathetic satellite glia are capable of reactive changes, specifically, enhanced gap junction-mediated coupling and increased ATP sensitivity.
source: Limited studies, so far, suggest that in response to nerve damage, sympathetic satellite glia are also capable of reactive changes, specifically, enhanced gap junction-mediated coupling and increased ATP sensitivity (Feldman-Goriachnik and Hanani, 2019), which, in turn, may augment neuronal activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Feldman-Goriachnik and Hanani, 2019.

claim: Satellite glia depletion or glial deletion of Kir4.1 resulted in the loss of approximately 25% of adult sympathetic neurons.
source: An intriguing finding was that satellite glia depletion or glial deletion of Kir4.1 resulted in the loss of ~25% of adult sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the neuronal loss data from BLBP:iDTA (24% decrease) and Kir4.1 cKO (22% decrease) mice.

claim: The exquisite dependence of sympathetic neurons on the target-derived survival factor, nerve growth factor (NGF), during development is well-documented.
source: The exquisite dependence of sympathetic neurons on the target-derived survival factor, nerve growth factor (NGF), during development is well-documented (Glebova and Ginty, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Glebova and Ginty, 2005.

claim: Loss of NGF signaling does not compromise the survival of adult sympathetic neurons.
source: However, loss of NGF signaling does not compromise the survival of adult neurons (Angeletti et al., 1971; Tsui-Pierchala and Ginty, 1999), and to date, the trophic mechanisms underlying adult sympathetic neuron survival in vivo remain undefined.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Angeletti et al., 1971 and Tsui-Pierchala and Ginty, 1999.

claim: The similar phenotypes of soma atrophy, impaired mTOR signaling, and enhanced apoptosis in adult BLBP:iDTA and Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic neurons suggest that satellite glia provide metabolic and trophic support to mature neurons, primarily, via regulation of K+ homeostasis.
source: The similar phenotypes of soma atrophy, impaired mTOR signaling, and enhanced apoptosis in adult BLBP:iDTA and Kir4.1 cKO sympathetic neurons suggest that satellite glia provide metabolic and trophic support to mature neurons, primarily, via regulation of K+ homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of phenotypes between BLBP:iDTA and Kir4.1 cKO mice.

claim: Astrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion results in defects in mTOR signaling and decreased soma size, but not cell death, in a population of spinal cord motor neurons.
source: Of note, astrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion also results in defects in mTOR signaling and decreased soma size, but not cell death, in a population of spinal cord motor neurons (Kelley et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kelley et al., 2018.

claim: Despite enhanced sympathetic neuron activity and circulating NE levels in satellite glia-ablated mice, there is a pronounced downregulation of NE biosynthetic machinery, specifically in neuronal cell bodies.
source: Further, despite enhanced sympathetic neuron activity and circulating NE levels in satellite glia-ablated mice, we observed a pronounced downregulation of NE biosynthetic machinery, specifically in neuronal cell bodies.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from the manuscript showing downregulated TH and DBH in soma despite elevated NE and activity.

claim: The downregulation of NE biosynthetic machinery in neuronal cell bodies may reflect a compensatory response to elevated sympathetic activity upon glia loss or the need for glia-derived factors in maintenance of noradrenergic enzymes.
source: This may reflect a compensatory response to elevated sympathetic activity upon glia loss or the need for glia-derived factors in maintenance of noradrenergic enzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms underlying the downregulation of NE biosynthetic enzymes.

claim: Satellite glia depletion resulted in soma-specific effects in sympathetic neurons, that is, TH downregulation and soma size decrease, without perturbing axonal TH levels and innervation.
source: It is also notable that satellite glia depletion resulted in soma-specific effects in sympathetic neurons, that is, TH downregulation and soma size decrease, without perturbing axonal TH levels and innervation.
evidence: This is a summary of observations comparing somatic versus axonal phenotypes in BLBP:iDTA mice.

claim: Th mRNA is trafficked to sympathetic axons, where it is locally translated.
source: Th mRNA is trafficked to sympathetic axons, where it is locally translated (Gervasi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gervasi et al., 2016.

claim: Enhanced Th mRNA trafficking and local synthesis might be a mechanism to maintain axonal TH expression and to locally regulate NE release in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic neurons.
source: Thus, enhanced Th mRNA trafficking and local synthesis might be a mechanism to maintain axonal TH expression and to locally regulate NE release in BLBP:iDTA sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms to maintain axonal TH despite somatic downregulation.

claim: Heightened activity of the sympathetic nervous system is a characteristic feature of several pathological conditions, specifically, chronic heart failure, arrhythmias, hypertension, sleep apnea, obesity, and insulin resistance.
source: Heightened activity of the sympathetic nervous system is a characteristic feature of several pathological conditions, specifically, chronic heart failure (Malpas, 2010), arrhythmias (Hasan, 2013; Schwartz, 2014), hypertension (Goldstein et al., 2002; Schlaich et al., 2004), sleep apnea, obesity, and insulin resistance (Mahfoud et al., 2011; Mancia et al., 2007; Schlaich et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Malpas, 2010; Hasan, 2013; Schwartz, 2014; Goldstein et al., 2002; Schlaich et al., 2004; Mahfoud et al., 2011; and Mancia et al., 2007.

claim: This study highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting the neuron–satellite glia unit in autonomic-related diseases.
source: While sympathetic neurons, so far, have been at the center stage in considering pathological mechanisms and treatments, our study, together with other recent work (Xie et al., 2017), highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting the neuron–satellite glia unit in autonomic-related diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications, with reference to another study (Xie et al., 2017).

claim: Satellite glia are the major glial cells in sympathetic ganglia, enveloping neuronal cell bodies.
source: Satellite glia are the major glial cells in sympathetic ganglia (Hanani, 2010; Mapps et al., 2021) and have a unique architecture in completely enveloping neuronal cell bodies (Elfvin and Forsman, 1978; Gabella et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hanani, 2010; Mapps et al., 2021; Elfvin and Forsman, 1978; and Gabella et al., 1988.

claim: Each neuron and associated glia are thought to form a discrete structural and functional unit.
source: Each neuron and associated glia are thought to form a discrete structural and functional unit (Hanani, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hanani, 2010.

claim: Satellite glial cells are derived from multipotent neural crest precursors.
source: Like neurons, satellite glial cells are derived from multipotent neural crest precursors and form thin cytoplasmic sheaths around cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses of sympathetic neurons, with only 20 nm of space, the width of a synaptic cleft, between neuronal and glial membranes (Elfvin and Forsman, 1978; Gabella et al., 1988; Hanani, 2010; Pannese, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elfvin and Forsman, 1978; Gabella et al., 1988; Hanani, 2010; and Pannese, 1981.

claim: Multiple satellite glia surround a single neuron and are connected with each other, and with neurons, via gap junctions, with the number of glial cells per neuron being positively correlated to soma size.
source: Multiple satellite glia surround a single neuron and are connected with each other, and with neurons, via gap junctions, with the number of glial cells per neuron being positively correlated to soma size (Elfvin and Forsman, 1978; Hanani, 2010; Ledda et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elfvin and Forsman, 1978; Hanani, 2010; and Ledda et al., 2004.

claim: Studies in sympathetic neuron–glia co-cultures have suggested roles for satellite glia in promoting dendrite growth, synapse formation, modulating extracellular ion and neurotransmitter concentrations, and regulating synaptic transmission.
source: Studies in sympathetic neuron–glia co-cultures have suggested roles for satellite glia in promoting dendrite growth, synapse formation, modulating extracellular ion and neurotransmitter concentrations, and regulating synaptic transmission (Enes et al., 2020; Feldman-Goriachnik et al., 2018; Hanani, 2010; Tropea et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Enes et al., 2020; Feldman-Goriachnik et al., 2018; Hanani, 2010; and Tropea et al., 1988.

claim: Recent studies implicate sensory satellite glia in regulating chronic pain through modulating neuronal hyper-excitability.
source: Recent studies implicate sensory satellite glia in regulating chronic pain through modulating neuronal hyper-excitability (Kim et al., 2016), and in promoting axon regeneration after peripheral nerve injury in vivo (Avraham et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2016 and Avraham et al., 2020.

claim: Satellite glia have been proposed to be closest to astrocytes in the central nervous system (CNS) with respect to expression of machinery related to neurotransmitter uptake/turnover, inward-rectifying potassium channels, functional coupling via gap junctions, and close association with synapses.
source: Satellite glia have been proposed to be closest to astrocytes in the central nervous system (CNS) with respect to expression of machinery related to neurotransmitter uptake/turnover, inward-rectifying potassium channels, functional coupling via gap junctions, and close association with synapses (Hanani and Spray, 2020; Hanani and Verkhratsky, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hanani and Spray, 2020 and Hanani and Verkhratsky, 2021.
